862.title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
862.hook: in the middle of the lament: God's mercies "are new every morning"
862.howItsDone: Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, thanks God for returning the soul and ends with the words of Lamentations 3:23, 'great is your faithfulness.'

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lamentations opened on a city sitting alone, tears on her cheeks. Your line was how she sits alone. Did you keep someone company? Today, a light comes on in the middle of that book. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

Halfway through Lamentations, a man speaks from what feels like the bottom of a pit. He says he's been led into darkness, hedged in so he can't get out, his prayers shut out. Line after line, it gets heavier. Then, with no warning, one sentence changes direction: "This I recall to my mind, Therefore have I hope." Nothing outside him has changed. The city is still in ruins. What changes is what he chooses to remember. Today's word is what he remembers.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE BOTTOM OF A PIT.` → `THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.` → `NOTHING OUTSIDE HAS CHANGED.`

segments.voice: New every morning. Here's what he recalls, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Surely the LORD's mercies are not consumed, Surely His compassions fail not. They are new every morning; Great is Thy faithfulness." Two words carry the weight. Mercies, in Hebrew chasadim: steady, loyal kindness, the kind that keeps a promise. And compassions, rachamim: tenderness, the way a parent feels toward a child. Those, he says, don't run out. They aren't stored up once, like grain in a barn, to be rationed until they're gone. They arrive fresh. A little like the manna in the wilderness, which came each morning and couldn't be saved for later. Then he adds: "The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; Therefore will I hope in Him." Now notice where all this sits. Not at the end of the book, as a happy ending. Right in the middle. The chapters before it mourn. The chapters after it mourn again. The hope doesn't erase the lament; the lament surrounds it on both sides. It's an honest shape for hope to take: not a door out of sorrow, but a lamp lit inside it. And the claim is small and daily. Not, everything is fine. Just: this morning, something was given that wasn't there last night. The phrase has traveled into the start of the Jewish day. Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, thanks God for returning the soul, and ends with these words from Lamentations: rabbah emunatecha, great is your faithfulness. A line from the ruins, said at dawn.
screen: `MERCIES AND COMPASSIONS FAIL NOT.` · `GIVEN FRESH, NOT STORED UP.` · then, large: `HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE LAMENT.` · then: `GREAT IS THY FAITHFULNESS, AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one new mercy today. Go back over the hours since you woke. Find one thing that was given to you today that you didn't earn and didn't plan: light through a window, a kind word, a body that got out of bed, a cup of something warm. Just one. Hold it for a moment, the way the voice in the pit held one memory. If you pray, you can say the old words from the verse: great is thy faithfulness. The bell holds the time.
New every morning. From the middle of Lamentations: God's mercies don't run out; they come fresh each morning. Today's word.
Your line: new every morning. Tonight, name one new mercy from today. Tomorrow when you wake, before you reach for your phone, look for the next one. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

863.title: Renew our days (Lamentations 5:21)
863.hook: the book's closing plea, "renew our days as of old", sung as the Torah returns to the ark
863.howItsDone: When Lamentations is read aloud on Tisha B'Av, the next-to-last verse is repeated after the final one, and 'hashivenu' is sung in synagogue as the Torah scroll is returned to the ark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the middle of Lamentations, mercies new every morning. Your line was new every morning. What new thing did you find? Today, the last lines of the book, and a custom that won't let it end where it ends. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

Some books end on a wedding, some on a homecoming. Lamentations ends on a verse that is hard to say out loud in a room full of mourners. The line just before it has had a longer life. Two weeks ago, this path heard the tree-of-life verses sung as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark. Right after them, as the doors close, comes this line, lifted from the last page of a book of ruins. Today's word is that line.
screen: `A HARD LAST VERSE.` → `THE LINE JUST BEFORE IT.` → `SUNG AS THE ARK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: Renew our days. The verse in full, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Turn Thou us unto Thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; Renew our days as of old." In Hebrew it begins hashivenu: turn us, bring us back. It asks for two things. First, turn us. Not, we will turn ourselves; turn us, and we will be turned. Then, renew our days as of old, kekedem, as before. Not a brand-new life. The old days, made new again. Now the hard part. That isn't the book's last verse. The last verse, in the same translation, reads: "Thou canst not have utterly rejected us, And be exceeding wroth against us!" The Hebrew is hard to pin down. Those translators heard a protest: surely you haven't cast us off for good. Other readers hear a plain statement that God has rejected them, or a fearful question left hanging. Either way, the book doesn't tie a bow. Jewish custom does something tender with that. When Lamentations is read aloud in public, the reader doesn't stop on the last verse. After it, the plea before it is said again: turn us, renew our days. So the congregation never closes the book on that cry. They close it on a request. The custom doesn't change a word of the text. It changes where the voice comes to rest. Even the JPS 1917 printing sets the plea again, in brackets, after the last verse. And the plea travels. When the Torah returns to the ark, the congregation sings hashivenu as the doors close. A line from a city in ruins becomes the line sung over a scroll going home. Renew our days: a plea that has already been through the worst, and still asks.
screen: `TURN US, AND WE SHALL BE TURNED.` · `THE OLD DAYS, MADE NEW.` · then, large: `THE LAST VERSE: CAST OFF FOR GOOD?` · then: `READERS REPEAT THE PLEA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for renewal. Think of one part of your life that has gone dry: a friendship, a habit you used to love, a way of paying attention that faded. Don't try to invent something new. Remember how it was when it was alive. Then ask, in whatever way you ask for things, for it to be renewed. If you pray, you can use the verse itself: renew our days as of old. The bell holds the time.
Renew our days. The plea near the end of Lamentations: turn us back, and make our days new, as of old. Today's word.
Your line: renew our days. Today, pick up one old good thing you'd let slip, and do it once more. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

864.title: Vashti refuses (Esther 1)
864.hook: a queen will not be put on display, and pays for it
864.howItsDone: The book of Esther is read aloud from a handwritten scroll on Purim, in the evening and again in the morning, beginning with the king's feast and Vashti's refusal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plea near the end of Lamentations: turn us back, renew our days. Your line was renew our days. What old good thing did you pick up again? Today, a new scroll opens, at a party in Persia. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

The party is in its seventh day. King Ahasuerus has already spent a hundred and eighty days, the text says, showing his officials the riches of his kingdom. Now everyone in the palace city of Shushan is invited. Wine is served in vessels of gold, as much as each guest pleases. On the seventh day, when the king's heart is merry with wine, he has one more thing to show. He sends seven chamberlains to bring in his queen. Today's word is what happened next.
screen: `A FEAST IN PERSIA.` → `THE KING'S HEART MERRY WITH WINE.` → `SEVEN CHAMBERLAINS SENT FOR THE QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Vashti refuses. The order, in the JPS 1917 translation, was to bring "Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to show the peoples and the princes her beauty; for she was fair to look on." She's to be brought in and shown, like the gold cups and the rest of the treasury. Then the next verse: "But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king's commandment by the chamberlains; therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him." In Hebrew it's quick: vatema'en, and she refused. The text never tells us why. It gives her no speech. Just the refusal, in one verb. What follows is almost comic. The king of the whole empire, furious, turns to his wise men and asks what the law says to do with a queen who won't come. One of them warns that word will spread, and wives across the kingdom will hear of it and despise their husbands. So letters go out to every province, to every people in its own language, that every man should bear rule in his own house. Vashti is to come no more before the king, and the search for a new queen begins. Readers have argued about Vashti for a long time. Some rabbinic stories paint her harshly. Some readers, especially in recent times, see a woman who would not be put on display, and paid for it. The text itself just sets down her no, and the cost. And it sets the stage: the empty seat beside the king is where the rest of this story will happen.
screen: `TO SHOW HER BEAUTY, LIKE THE TREASURY.` · `VATEMA'EN: AND SHE REFUSED.` · then, large: `LETTERS TO EVERY PROVINCE.` · then: `READERS STILL ARGUE ABOUT HER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect someone's no. Think of a recent time someone told you no: a friend who couldn't come, a child who wouldn't, a colleague who drew a line. Notice how it felt to hear it, without arguing it again. Then think of someone whose no you might be pushing against right now. What would it look like to let their no stand, without a decree, without making them pay for it? If you pray, you can ask for the grace to hear no well. The bell holds the time.
Vashti refuses. The queen will not be brought in to be shown off, and the king's anger burns. Today's word.
Your line: vashti said no. Today, when someone tells you no, take it the first time, and thank them for being clear. Day eight hundred sixty-four.

865.title: She didn't tell (Esther 2)
865.hook: Esther keeps her people and her kindred to herself at the palace
865.howItsDone: On Purim the scroll of Esther is chanted in synagogue, and the custom of dressing in costume is linked by some to the way Esther's identity stays hidden in the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Queen Vashti refused to be put on display, and lost her place. Your line was vashti said no. Whose no did you respect? Today, the empty seat is filled, by a young woman with a secret. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

She has two names. The book introduces her as Hadassah, that is, Esther. She has neither father nor mother. Her cousin Mordecai, the text says, took her for his own daughter. Then the king's officers gather young women from across the empire to the palace, and she is taken too. And at that moment the book stops to tell us about something she doesn't say. Today's word is her silence.
screen: `HADASSAH, THAT IS, ESTHER.` → `RAISED BY HER COUSIN MORDECAI.` → `SOMETHING SHE DOESN'T SAY.`

segments.voice: She didn't tell. In the JPS 1917 translation: "Esther had not made known her people nor her kindred; for Mordecai had charged her that she should not tell it." She's in the house of the women, in the care of the king's chamberlain Hegai, and nobody there knows she's a Jew. The text doesn't say why Mordecai asked this of her. It lets you feel the danger without naming it. Then comes a small detail that's easy to miss. Every day, Mordecai walks in front of the court of the women's house, to know how Esther did, and what would become of her. The text doesn't say he goes in. He walks past, every day, just to know how she is. When her turn comes to go to the king, she asks for nothing beyond what Hegai advises. The king loves her above all the women and sets the royal crown on her head. A great feast is held, Esther's feast. And then the book says it again, almost word for word: "Esther had not yet made known her kindred nor her people; as Mordecai had charged her." Now she's queen, and still she hasn't told. The repetition is the point. The crown didn't change the secret. She keeps it in the women's house, and she keeps it on the throne. In this story the silence reads less like shame than like waiting: one true thing held close until the day it's needed. The book doesn't say yet when that day will come. For now: she didn't tell. Not yet.
screen: `SHE HAD NOT MADE KNOWN HER PEOPLE.` · `MORDECAI WALKS PAST EVERY DAY.` · then, large: `CROWNED, AND STILL SHE HASN'T TOLD.` · then: `ONE TRUE THING, KEPT CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what you keep hidden. Ask yourself, gently: what part of who I am do I keep quiet in certain rooms? A belief, a background, a language, a grief, a hope. You don't have to decide whether keeping it quiet is wise. Just notice it, and notice where you keep it. Then think of one place, or one person, where it would be safe to be seen. If you pray, you can bring what's hidden there too. The bell holds the time.
She didn't tell. Esther keeps her people and her kindred to herself, even after the crown. Today's word.
Your line: she didn't tell. Today, notice one thing you're holding back, and one person you might trust with it someday. Day eight hundred sixty-five.

866.title: He bowed not (Esther 3)
866.hook: Mordecai won't bow to Haman, and Haman plots against all the Jews
866.tomorrow: For such a time as this (Esther 4:14)
866.howItsDone: When the scroll of Esther is read on Purim, it is a custom to drown out Haman's name with noisemakers and stamping each time it is read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esther kept her people and her kindred to herself, even after the crown. Your line was she didn't tell. What did you notice you keep close? Today, her cousin does something very different, at the king's gate. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

The king's gate in Shushan. King Ahasuerus has just raised a man named Haman above all the princes, and given an order: when Haman passes, the king's servants bow. So at the gate, they bow. Officials, servants, the whole row of them bending low as he walks by. Except one man, who stays standing. He's the same man who once walked past the women's court every day to ask after Esther. Now he stands still while everyone else bends. Today's word is what he didn't do.
screen: `THE KING'S GATE IN SHUSHAN.` → `WHEN HAMAN PASSES, EVERYONE BOWS.` → `ONE MAN STAYS STANDING.`

segments.voice: He bowed not. The verse, in the JPS 1917 translation: "And all the king's servants, that were in the king's gate, bowed down, and prostrated themselves before Haman; for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai bowed not down, nor prostrated himself before him." Day after day the servants ask him why he breaks the king's command. He gives no speech. What the text says he told them is this: that he was a Jew. That's the only reason the book offers, and it doesn't explain further. Later readers supplied reasons of their own. Some midrashic stories say Haman wore an idol, so bowing to him meant bowing to it. Others read it as Mordecai refusing to give a man the honor he owed to God alone. The text leaves the why at the edge and puts the weight on the act. Notice the turn. Yesterday Esther kept who she was hidden. Today Mordecai says it out loud, and it costs. When Haman sees that Mordecai bows not, he is full of wrath. And the story darkens. Haman thinks it beneath him to strike at Mordecai alone. He seeks to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. Lots are cast before him, pur, to choose the day. Then he goes to the king and describes a certain people, scattered among the provinces, whose laws are different. The king hands over his ring. Letters go out. And the chapter ends with two pictures side by side: "the king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Shushan was perplexed." The powerful drink. The city is bewildered. Haman's anger at one man who would not bend has turned on a whole people.
screen: `ALL THE KING'S SERVANTS BOWED.` · `HE TOLD THEM HE WAS A JEW.` · then, large: `HAMAN'S WRATH TURNS ON A PEOPLE.` · then: `THE CITY OF SHUSHAN WAS PERPLEXED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand upright once. If you're able, stand up now; if not, sit as tall as is comfortable. Let your feet find the floor. Lift gently through the top of your head, shoulders easy, and breathe. Notice what it feels like to take up your full height. Then think of one place in your life where you bend when you'd rather stand: a joke you laugh along with, a word you swallow. You don't have to change it today. Just stand, and feel what upright is. If you pray, you can pray standing. The bell holds the time.
He bowed not. Mordecai stays standing when everyone at the king's gate bows to Haman. Today's word.
Your line: he bowed not. Today, in one small moment, say plainly who you are or what you think, kindly and without a fight. Day eight hundred sixty-six.

screen: `DAY 866 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.`

867.title: For such a time as this (Esther 4:14)
867.word: For such a time as this
867.hook: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?"
867.carry: for such a time as this
867.howItsDone: Esther 9:22 names how the days of Purim are to be kept, with feasting and joy, sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor, and Purim is still kept with a festive meal, gifts of food to friends, and gifts to the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole gate bowed to Haman, and one man stayed standing. Your line was he bowed not. Where did you stay upright, even a little? Today, the news of Haman's decree reaches the palace. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

The news reaches the queen secondhand. Her maids come and tell Esther that Mordecai is outside the king's gate in sackcloth and ashes. In every province where the decree has gone, the text says, there's mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping. Esther sends Mordecai clothes. He won't put them on. So the messages begin, carried back and forth by a servant named Hatach. Mordecai sends a copy of the decree and asks her to go to the king and plead for her people. Esther's answer is careful, and it's true. Anyone who walks into the inner court without being called is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter. And she hasn't been called, she says, for thirty days. Then Mordecai sends back an answer, and it ends in a question.
screen: `SACKCLOTH OUTSIDE THE GATE.` → `MESSAGES THROUGH HATACH.` → `NOT CALLED FOR THIRTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: He starts bluntly. In the King James words: "Think not with thyself that thou shalt escape in the king's house, more than all the Jews." The palace walls won't hide her. Then he says something stranger. If she stays silent, help will still come to the Jews, from another place. Mordecai doesn't think the rescue depends on her alone. The question is whether she'll be part of it. And then, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" Notice it's a question. Who knows. Mordecai doesn't promise her it will work. He doesn't tell her she was born for this. He only asks her to consider that the strange road that brought her here, the orphan raised by her cousin, the girl taken into the palace, the queen who kept her people a secret, might have been leading to this one moment. The thing that kept her safe and quiet is the very thing that gives her a voice now. Some readers linger on that phrase, from another place. The book of Esther is a story where help arrives through ordinary people, timing and nerve, and some readers hear in another place a quiet hint of God. Others hear simply that the people will survive somehow. Either way, the question lands on Esther. A palace is far from a kitchen. But there may be a place where you stand, a meeting, a family table, a group chat, a classroom, where you could say a thing that needs saying.
screen: `THE PALACE WON'T HIDE HER.` · `HELP WILL COME FROM ANOTHER PLACE.` · `WHO KNOWETH: A QUESTION, NOT A PROMISE.` · then, large: `FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.` · then: `THE HIDDEN QUEEN, IN THE RIGHT ROOM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to step up for one thing. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Walk in your mind through the places you'll stand this week: a desk, a kitchen, a phone, a team, a family. Go slowly. In one of them, there may be something you're placed to say or do. Not the whole rescue. One thing. A word to the right person. A call you've been putting off. Don't decide yet. Just set Mordecai's question beside it: who knows whether you're here for this. If you pray, you can bring it to God in words from your tradition, or in silence. The bell holds the time.
For such a time as this. Mordecai's question to Esther: maybe this moment is why you reached the palace at all. Today's word.
screen: `FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for such a time as this. Today, do the one thing you found, or the first small piece of it, before evening. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.

868.title: If I perish (Esther 4:16, 7)
868.hook: Esther says "if I perish, I perish", and names the enemy at her banquet
868.howItsDone: The day before Purim is kept by tradition as the Fast of Esther, Ta'anit Esther, which recalls the fast she asked of the Jews of Shushan before she went in to the king.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mordecai asked Esther who knows whether she came to the palace for such a time as this. Your line was for such a time as this. Did you do your one thing? Today, Esther answers, and the week ends. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

Esther's reply is short, and it's an order. Go, gather all the Jews in Shushan, and fast for me. Don't eat or drink for three days, night or day. My maids and I will fast too. Then I'll go in to the king, which is not according to the law. And she ends with a line that sounds almost like a shrug: "and if I perish, I perish." Something has flipped. Back in chapter two, Mordecai gave the orders and Esther kept quiet. Now the text says Mordecai went his way and "did according to all that Esther had commanded him."

segments.voice: If I perish, I perish. It isn't despair. It's a person counting the cost before she moves, and then moving. Esther doesn't pretend the danger is small. She names it, prepares, and goes. On the third day she puts on her royal clothes and stands in the inner court. The king sees her, and holds out the golden scepter. She lives. He offers her anything, up to half the kingdom. And here's the surprise: she doesn't blurt out her request. She invites the king and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet, she invites them to another one. Some readers call it stalling. Others call it strategy: she's choosing the room, the hour, and the moment the king is ready to listen. At the second banquet, chapter seven, she finally speaks, and she ties her own life to her people's: "let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request." The secret she kept since chapter two, who her people are, is out loud now. "For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish." Perish again, the same word she risked for herself. The king asks who would dare. And she names him to his face: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman." Before the chapter ends, Haman is hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The story still has chapters to run, but the turn happens here, at a dinner table, when one person says the name.

And today's answer. Now the practice: speak up for someone. Bring to mind one person who isn't in the room when things about them get decided. A coworker, a neighbor, a child, someone easy to forget. What would you say for them, if you were asked? Find the sentence. Make it plain and kind and true. Esther took three days to get ready; you have the length of the bell.
